summary:
The challenge. SPHEREx returns to every part of the sky about twice a year, so its images hold a record of what changes: stars that move, stars that brighten and fade, and faint objects such as nearby brown dwarfs. That record is spread over hundreds of large files per spot in NASA's archive, with no simple way to compare them.

What TimeLens does: Type a star's name or sky coordinates. TimeLens finds every SPHEREx exposure of that spot, cuts a small, aligned piece out of each original file, and groups the exposures into visits. You can then:

see motion by blinking or playing the visits, or subtracting one from another;
see brightness change across visits and read the star's spectrum over the 102 colours;
let it hunt for movers, with every find checked against the Gaia DR3 catalogue and kept as a candidate for you to review, never announced as a discovery.
How it stays trustworthy. Every picture is a real SPHEREx exposure, cut from the original file at SPHEREx's own pixel size. Pixels SPHEREx flagged or left blank are shown as such and never filled in. Each number links back to its source (release, file, pipeline version), and the app is checked against reference values. For example, Barnard's Star should move about 10.4″ a year, matching Gaia. See docs/SCIENCE_RULES.md.

Who it is for. Students, amateur astronomers and anyone curious: no account, download or astronomy software is needed.
details:
What it does: SPHEREx TimeLens is a free web app that turns NASA’s SPHEREx images into a time-lapse anyone can explore. SPHEREx maps the whole sky about every six months in 102 colours of infrared light, so its images record how the sky changes: stars that move, stars that brighten and fade, and faint nearby brown dwarfs. That record is spread over hundreds of large files (about 70 MB each) per spot, in an archive built for experts. TimeLens makes it easy to see. You type a star’s name or sky coordinates, and the app shows every SPHEREx picture of that spot, lined up in time.

How it works:

  1. It turns the name into a sky position with NASA’s MAST service (SIMBAD and NED).
  2. It finds every SPHEREx exposure of that spot through NASA’s IRSA archive. If IRSA is down, it falls back to IRSA’s table search, then to our own index of NASA’s copy on AWS.
  3. Instead of downloading whole files, it reads only the small piece it needs from each one. It then aligns every piece on the same grid, with north up, at SPHEREx’s own pixel size.
  4. It groups the exposures into visits, which you can explore in four modes:
    • Time: blink, play, subtract or combine visits to see motion.
    • Spectrum: brightness across all 102 colours and over time, downloadable as CSV.
    • Movers: the app flags what moved between visits and checks each find against ESA’s Gaia DR3 catalogue.
    • Sky: all visits added together into the deepest picture.

Benefits and intended impact: SPHEREx data is public, but until now only professionals could really use it. TimeLens opens it to students, teachers, amateur astronomers and anyone curious. You need only a web browser: no account, no download and no astronomy software. Every view is a shareable link that opens exactly what you see, so others can check a find. The goal is to let more people take part in exploring NASA’s newest all-sky mission and its search for moving and changing objects.

Tools and languages:

  • Backend: Python, with FastAPI, Uvicorn, httpx, Astropy, NumPy, reproject and Pillow.
  • Frontend: JavaScript with React 19 and Vite, plus Tailwind CSS, React Router, TanStack Query, Zustand and Motion. Images are drawn with Canvas and a Web Worker.
  • Data: NASA SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 (via IRSA and AWS Open Data), Gaia DR3, CatWISE2020, MAST, and the SPHEREx all-sky map shown with Aladin Lite.
  • Testing: pytest, Vitest and Playwright.

How it’s creative:

  • It turns a professional archive into something you can play like a time-lapse.
  • The home page shows the real SPHEREx sky in false colour, built from three of its infrared wavelengths. It moves with your cursor for a sense of depth.
  • A seven-step guided tour takes newcomers from searching for a star to hunting for movers.

Factors our team considered:

  • Scientific honesty: we use real data only. Nothing is simulated, missing pixels stay blank, and every number shows where it came from. Finds are called candidates, never discoveries, and brown dwarfs are clearly marked as not stars.
  • Accuracy: we checked results against NASA’s original files with Astropy. Star positions agree to within 0.0007 of a pixel, wavelengths to within 0.005 nm, and raw pixels and flags are identical.
  • Reliability: backup search routes keep the app working when NASA’s archive is down, and the five challenge targets are pre-built so they open instantly.
  • Accessibility: the app works by keyboard, keeps readable contrast, respects “reduce motion” settings, and works on phones.
  • Speed: small byte-range reads instead of full downloads
